title: Bonito
translation: Bonito, the fish from the sea at Kamakura, is the best thing around there, and these days it's very much in fashion. But an old man from Kamakura told me: "When we were young, this fish never went near the table of anyone who mattered. Not even the servants ate the head. We cut it off and threw it away."
As the world goes downhill, even a fish like that ends up on the best tables.
original: {鎌倉|かまくら}の{海|うみ}にかつをといふ{魚|うを}は、かの{境|さかひ}には{双|さう}なきものにて、この{頃|ごろ}もてなすものなり。
それも{鎌倉|かまくら}の{年寄|としより}の{申|まう}し{侍|はべ}りしは、「この{魚|うを}おのれ{等|ら}{若|わか}かりし{世|よ}までは、はかばかしき{人|ひと}の{前|まへ}へ{出|い}づること{侍|はべ}らざりき。{頭|かしら}は{下部|しもべ}も{食|く}はず、{切|き}り{捨|す}て{侍|はべ}りしものなり。」と{申|まう}しき。
かやうの{物|もの}も、{世|よ}の{末|すゑ}になれば、{上|うへ}ざままでも{入|い}りたつわざにこそ{侍|はべ}れ。
literal: The fish called katsuo in the sea at Kamakura is unequalled in that region, and these days it is much made of.

As for that, too, an old man of Kamakura said: 'Until the time when we were young, this fish never appeared before people of standing. The head not even servants ate; it was a thing we cut off and threw away.'
Things like this too, when the world comes to its latter days, make their way even into the upper classes.

notes.text: Katsuo, skipjack tuna, usually called bonito in English. Later, in the Edo period, the first katsuo of the season became a famous luxury.
Kamakura, the seat of the shogunate, the military government, from the late twelfth century until 1333. Kenkō spent time in the region himself (see section 34).
{双|さう}なし: 'without equal'. Section 118 uses the same word for the pheasant.
き: the old man speaks of what he saw himself. Kenkō, in turn, closes the quotation with {申|まう}しき: he heard it himself.

'The end of the world', the latter days. Buddhist teaching said the world was in a period of decline, and Kenkō and his readers often blamed the times for changes they did not like. Compare section 22.

notes.quote: 入りたつわざにこそ侍れ
notes.text: こそ … {侍|はべ}れ: the realis form closes the こそ. {上|うへ}ざま: 'the upper ranks'.
